## Light Propagation Through a Changing Yield

For lightlike propagation along the selected direction, the directed momentum fraction has unit magnitude. In the forward orientation,

$$
\frac{p_k}{M(p)}=1,
$$

and the translation map becomes

$$
\boxed{
\dot x(t)=\chi(t)c
}.
$$

This is a lightlike translation statement. It says how rapidly lightlike momentum lays down displacement in the background propagation coordinate. It does not say that the signal's bosic momentum changes in flight, and it does not replace intrinsic $c$ with a second fundamental constant. At any epoch, $c$ retains its local role; $\chi(t)$ tells how the background converts that lightlike expression into accumulated displacement.

A signal emitted at $t_e$ and observed at $t_o$ therefore samples a history, not only a value at one endpoint. Along a one-dimensional propagation path, its accumulated background interval is

$$
\mathcal D_\chi(t_e,t_o)
=
c\int_{t_e}^{t_o}\chi(t)\,dt.
$$

The symbol $\mathcal D_\chi$ denotes the translation interval generated by the yield history. It is not yet a measured ruler distance, luminosity distance, angular-diameter distance, or complete observational distance. Those require local standards, geometry, and observer bookkeeping.

The distinction between the integral and its endpoints is essential. The full history determines how much translation the signal accumulates. The endpoint values,

$$
\chi_e=\chi(t_e),
\qquad
\chi_o=\chi(t_o),
$$

enter when neighboring signal features or locally established intervals are compared between emission and observation.

Consider two neighboring features emitted by the same source and received by the same observer. During their short separation, take the source and observer to maintain the same background-coordinate separation, and neglect peculiar motion, lensing changes, and inhomogeneity along the path. The two features then follow the same coordinate path through the same homogeneous background, but over slightly shifted time intervals. If the first travels from $t_e$ to $t_o$ and the second from $t_e+\delta t_e$ to $t_o+\delta t_o$, their equal path constraint is

$$
c\int_{t_e}^{t_o}\chi(t)\,dt
=
c\int_{t_e+\delta t_e}^{t_o+\delta t_o}\chi(t)\,dt.
$$

For neighboring features, with $\chi$ varying negligibly across each endpoint interval, the first-order difference gives

$$
\chi_o\delta t_o
=
\chi_e\delta t_e.
$$

This result is operationally narrower than a complete redshift theory. It relates shifts of neighboring emission and reception events in the common background parameter. Reading those shifts as locally reported durations requires matched endpoint clock standards. Assigning a wavelength to the transported signal pattern likewise requires a rule for comparison with local length standards.

The propagation engine has therefore supplied the history and endpoint timing relation. The next section attaches the conditional signal dictionary that connects those quantities to measured wavelength and duration.
